subject: mathematics
question_text: Find the sum of the infinite terms of the G.P. 1/3, −2/9, 4/27, −8/81, …

mark_split.label: Find a and r and check that |r| < 1

recall_prompt: Say how you would do this one — say what the common ratio is, sign included, and what has to be true before the infinite sum formula can be used.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Find a and r and check that |r| < 1
steps.margin_note: First mark. Both the negative ratio and the |r| < 1 check earn it. Divide the second term by the first, never the first by the second.
steps.memory_tip: Signs that alternate mean r is negative; the size of r decides whether the infinite sum exists.
lines: |r| = 2/3 < 1, so the infinite sum exists and S∞ = a/(1 − r)

recall.must_convey: That a = 1/3, r = −2/3, and |r| < 1 so S∞ = a/(1 − r) may be used.
accept: the first term is one third and the ratio is minus two thirds
divide the second term by the first to get the ratio
the terms alternate in sign so r is negative
modulus r one kanna thakkuva unte sum untundi
check the modulus of r is less than one before using the formula

steps.why: The sign of r has to be carried, because the terms alternate. The condition |r| < 1 is what allows the infinite sum formula to be used at all, so it is written before the formula.
common_mistakes: Taking r as +2/3 and losing the alternating signs.
Using a/(1 − r) without stating that |r| < 1.

steps.label: Substitute in a/(1 − r)
steps.margin_note: Second mark. The double negative in 1 − r is where marks are lost. The answer is positive and smaller than the first term, which is a fair check.
steps.memory_tip: Subtracting a negative ratio makes the denominator larger than 1.

accept: one minus minus two thirds is five thirds
one third divided by five thirds is one fifth
the two minus signs make a plus in the denominator
minus minus plus avuthundi, so five by three vasthundi

steps.why: 1 − (−2/3) becomes 1 + 2/3 = 5/3, because the two minus signs make a plus. Dividing by 5/3 is the same as multiplying by 3/5, and the 3s cancel.
common_mistakes: Writing 1 − 2/3 = 1/3 and getting 1 as the sum.
Leaving the answer as one fraction divided by another instead of simplifying.
